data.caption: earthscure.com
data.copy:
Nobody tells you about retiring as a teacher.

For 40 years, I was looked at all day, every day.

Twenty-five 8-year-olds, watching everything. Parents at pickup. The principal in the doorway. Open house nights.

I was never a fancy woman. But for 40 years, I was a put-together one, because tons of little eyes made sure of it.

Then I retired at sixty-one.

And the version of what happened next that you could say out loud sounded fine.

More time with the grandkids. The garden. Church on Sundays.

The version I had been living with was harder to put into words.

It looked like this.

It looked like the drawer in my bathroom, full of makeup that had all, one by one, quietly stopped working. The eyeliner that started reading harsh instead of neat, the foundation that looked alright at eight in the morning and had settled into the lines around my mouth by lunch.

I kept them in my drawer thinking maybe one day I'll try makeup again.

It reminds me of all the little boys and girls that I would teach all day.

It reminds me of my daughter's wedding. My granddaughter's first birthday.

But somewhere along the way, the makeup just started looking worse and worse. It started to remind me of the pictures that my face was too done up. Or the pictures that my foundation was cracked to pieces.

So I had given up on makeup entirely. Going down to just moisturizer and chapstick, which I told myself was a choice. Which I told myself was natural. Which I told myself "that's what a retired woman does."

So now. I wear no makeup. Which also comes with its own challenges.

I was in the produce section, no makeup, hair pushed back, in the clothes I'd worn to weed the garden.

A woman about forty-years-old came around the corner with her cart, stopped, and said: Mrs. Hoffman?

One of my third graders. Class of maybe 1993. She'd have been seven the last time she sat in my room.

She was so happy to see me. She hugged me. She told me I was her favorite teacher.

data.caption: acepillow.com
data.copy:
I was 59 years old when I scheduled an appointment with a neurologist because I thought I had early-onset dementia. Forgetting words mid-sentence. Walking into rooms with no idea why. Struggling to focus on anything past 2 PM.

Turns out, it wasn't my brain dying. It was something happening to my neck while I slept.

Let me explain.

I used to be sharp. The one in meetings who always had the answer. The one who remembered every detail, every name, every deadline.

Somewhere around my 57th birthday, that person disappeared.

It started small. Losing my train of thought mid-conversation. Reading the same email 3 times without absorbing it. Standing in the grocery store unable to remember what I came for.

Then it got worse.

I forgot the word "calendar" during a presentation. Just stood there pointing at the wall while 14 colleagues stared at me.

I got lost driving to my dentist's office. An office I'd been going to for 8 years.

I started writing everything down because I couldn't trust my own brain anymore.

By 3 PM every day, I was useless. Staring at my computer screen, unable to process simple tasks. Drinking my 4th coffee just to feel half-awake.

I thought this was just aging. Just what 59 felt like.

Then my husband said something that terrified me.

"You asked me the same question three times in 10 minutes yesterday. You didn't remember asking it."

That's when I called the neurologist.

I sat in her office convinced she was going to diagnose me with early-onset Alzheimer's. I'd already started grieving the person I used to be.

She ran tests. MRI. Cognitive assessments. Blood work.

Everything came back normal.

"Your brain looks fine," she said. "But I want to ask you something. How do you sleep?"

I told her. The snoring. The gasping at night. The exhaustion every morning no matter how many hours I was in bed.

She nodded slowly. "Have you ever had a sleep study?"

I hadn't. I thought snoring was just annoying, not dangerous.

I found something at Walmart last Tuesday that changed my life.

I wasn't looking for it. I went in for cat litter and a rotisserie chicken.

I came out with a bag of cat litter, a rotisserie chicken, and a piece of paper that a stranger handed me in the checkout line. A folded receipt with three words written on the back in blue ballpoint pen.

I still have it. It's on my fridge, under the magnet from my granddaughter's dance recital. I look at it every morning when I make coffee.

Three words.

I'll tell you what they were in a minute.

But first I have to back up, because if I just tell you what was on the paper without telling you what came before it, you won't understand why a folded receipt from a stranger made me sit in my car in the Walmart parking lot and cry for fifteen minutes before I could drive home.

My name is Jessica. I'm 57 years old. I live in a small town outside Chattanooga called Soddy Daisy, which I know sounds made up but I promise you it's real. Look it up. We have a Dollar General and two churches and a Sonic and that's about it.

I've been married to my husband Wendell for 34 years. He's 61. He drove a delivery route for the same bread company for 28 years, retired three years ago, and has been quietly disappearing ever since.

That's the only word I have for it. Disappearing.

Not all at once. Not in a way you'd notice from the outside.

But when you've slept next to a man for 34 years, you know the shape of him. You know what his footsteps sound like in the kitchen at 6:15 in the morning. You know how loud he laughs at the same Andy Griffith reruns we've been watching since the kids were little. You know which side of the bed he sleeps on and how heavy his arm feels when he reaches over in his sleep.

And one day you start to notice that all of those things have gotten quieter. Lighter. Fainter.

The footsteps got slower. The laugh got shorter. The arm stopped reaching over.

data.caption: Week 24: The Drusen Kept Shrinking
data.copy:
Twenty four weeks ago I posted my first update. You asked me to keep going. I kept going. Here are the numbers.

My name is Liam. I am seventy two years old. I was a certified public accountant for forty three years in Hartford, Connecticut.

If you read my first post at week twelve, you already know the basics. If this is the first time you are seeing my name, I will bring you up to speed in about thirty seconds.

I was diagnosed with intermediate dry age related macular degeneration in October of last year. Eleven drusen deposits in the left macula, six in the right. Largest drusen measured 167 microns in the left eye.

I started a supplement called Visiovance 15 in 1 Advanced Eye Formula on January 10th. I have not missed a single morning capsule since.

At week twelve my largest drusen had dropped from 167 microns to 142 microns. I posted the scan results. I told you I would come back at week twenty four.

I am back.

Let me tell you something about a promise made by a CPA.

When I wrote that first update at week twelve I was careful about what I promised. I did not promise improvement. I did not promise the drusen would keep shrinking. I did not promise anything about the supplement at all.

What I promised was that I would keep taking the capsule every morning, keep filling in the ledger every night, go back for the next OCT scan at week twenty four, and report the results exactly as the machine printed them.

That is a documentation promise. That is the only kind of promise I know how to make.

So here I am at week twenty four with the ledger open in front of me, the scan printout sitting on my desk next to the two previous scans, and a cup of coffee getting cold because I wanted to write this before I did anything else today.

Let me walk you through what the last twelve weeks of the ledger look like, because the ledger is the whole story.

data.caption: Does Your Bible Ever Feel Overwhelming?
data.copy:
This is going to sound strange, but I used to be scared of my own Bible.

Not scared of it in some dramatic way. It was quieter than that. I would sit down with good intentions, open to wherever I'd left off, and somewhere in the middle of reading I'd hit a verse about judgment or wrath or falling away, and my whole body would just tense up. I'd read the same sentence four or five times, trying to figure out if it meant something specific about me.

I never told anyone that part. It felt embarrassing to admit that the thing I was supposed to find comfort in was the thing making my chest feel tight.

It started small, honestly. A verse here and there that I couldn't quite let go of. I'd close my Bible and instead of feeling closer to God, I'd feel unsettled for the rest of the day, replaying the verse in my head, wondering if I was somehow on the wrong side of it.

Some mornings I noticed my hands would actually get a little tense before I even opened it. Like some part of me was bracing for whatever I was about to read.

I remember one specific night, I read something in one of the Prophets, I don't even remember which book exactly, something about judgment coming on a nation that had turned away, and I spiraled for hours after that. Not because anything in my actual life had changed. Just because I couldn't stop turning the verse over, trying to figure out what it meant, whether it applied to me somehow, whether I was missing some warning I was supposed to take seriously.

I started avoiding certain books altogether. Anything with the word judgment in the summary, I'd just skip past it. Which felt wrong too, because I knew I was supposed to be reading the whole thing, not just the comfortable parts.

There was a night I actually said something out loud to my husband about it, just kind of blurted it out, that reading my Bible sometimes made me feel worse instead of better. He didn't really know what to say, and honestly neither did I. It felt like a strange thing t…

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
